passages.text: Nevertheless, if anyone surveys the whole accurately by reason, he will find that God has made it for the sake of humankind. For rainstorms occur for the sake of crops, so that a human may partake of them and animals may be fed so that they may serve humankind. The sun also shines and turns the air through four seasonal changes, so that each season may furnish humankind with what belongs to it. Springs also gush forth so that drink may be given to humans. Moreover, who, to the extent possible, exercises dominion over creation? Is it not the human being, who has received wisdom to cultivate the earth, sail the sea, hunt swimming creatures, flying creatures, and wild beasts, calculate the course of the stars, mine the earth, sift the sea, raise cities, appoint kings, establish laws, judge, conceive of an invisible God, know the names of angels, drive out demons, attempt to stop diseases with medicines, discover incantations against venomous reptiles, and devise natural counteragents?

lexical_decisions.chosen: surveys the whole accurately by reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὸ πᾶν denotes the whole created order under consideration, while λογισμός indicates rational reflection.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν ἀέρα εἰς τέσσαρας τροπὰς τρέπει
lexical_decisions.chosen: turns the air through four seasonal changes
lexical_decisions.rationale: The four τροπαί are clarified by the following reference to each καιρός; “four turnings” is a more literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: hunt swimming creatures, flying creatures, and wild beasts
lexical_decisions.rationale: The asyndetic accusatives name three classes of creatures subject to human hunting.

lexical_decisions.chosen: sift the sea
lexical_decisions.rationale: σήθειν literally means to sift or strain; the unusual image of searching or working the sea is retained.

lexical_decisions.chosen: devise natural counteragents
lexical_decisions.rationale: In the context of venomous reptiles, ἀντιπάθειαι are opposing natural properties or remedies; “antipathies” would obscure that practical sense.

passages.text: If you were grateful, human being, having recognized the God who benefited you in everything, you too would be immortal, with the things created for your sake continuing to exist because of your gratitude. Even now, however, you can become incorruptible, if you recognize the one you failed to notice, if you love the one you abandoned, and if you pray to him alone, who is able to punish and save your body and soul. Therefore, above all, consider that no one rules together with him and no one shares his designation—namely, that which is called “God.” For he alone is both called God and is God, and it is permitted neither to regard another as God nor to call another God. If anyone should dare to do so, that person’s soul is destined to be punished eternally.

lexical_decisions.chosen: If you were grateful
lexical_decisions.rationale: The imperfect with ἂν ἦς forms a counterfactual condition; εὐγνωμονεῖν here is gratitude toward the benefactor.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν διὰ σὲ κτισθέντων δι’ εὐγνωμοσύνην τὸ διαμένειν ἐχόντων
lexical_decisions.chosen: with the things created for your sake continuing to exist because of your gratitude
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive absolute links the continuance of created things to the human being’s gratitude; the precise causal conception remains the author’s own.

lexical_decisions.chosen: no one shares his designation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὀνομασία denotes the designation or name subsequently identified as “God.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄλλον δὲ οὔτε νομίσαι οὔτε εἰπεῖν ἔξεστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: it is permitted neither to regard another as God nor to call another God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The preceding discussion supplies “God” as the complement of both verbs; νομίζειν can also be rendered “acknowledge” or “consider.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: that person’s soul is destined to be punished eternally
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔχει with the infinitive expresses an impending or necessary consequence, not possession.

passages.text: When Peter had said these things, Simon, from outside the crowd, said in a loud voice, “Why do you wish, by lying, to deceive the uninstructed crowd standing with you, persuading it that it is permitted neither to regard any as gods nor to call them gods, when the public books among the Jews say that there are many gods? Even now, before everyone, I wish to debate with you from those very books about whether gods ought to be acknowledged. But first I will demonstrate that the god of whom you spoke is not the highest power capable of everything, since he lacks foreknowledge, is incomplete, is needy, is not good, and is subject to many—indeed, countless—painful passions. Consequently, when this has been demonstrated from the Scriptures, as I maintain, another remains, without being written of, who possesses foreknowledge, is perfect, needs nothing, is good, and is free from all painful passions. But the one whom you call the Creator proves to be subject to the opposite qualities.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: uninstructed crowd
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἰδιώτης here characterizes the crowd as lacking specialist knowledge; “ordinary” or “lay” are possible alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: neither to regard any as gods nor to call them gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: νομίζειν concerns acknowledgment or recognition, while λέγειν concerns naming or speaking of them as gods.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the public books among the Jews
lexical_decisions.rationale: δημόσιοι presents the books as public or commonly recognized; rendering it “canonical” would add a later technical category.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he lacks foreknowledge
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπρόγνωστος negates prior knowledge; “without foreknowledge” is an equally direct alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: another remains, without being written of
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀγράφως may mean that this other deity is unattested in writing or inferred apart from the written accounts; the former is adopted in context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πολλοῖς καὶ μυρίοις χαλεποῖς ὑποκείμενος πάθεσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: subject to many—indeed, countless—painful passions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both πολλοῖς and the intensifying μυρίοις, while πάθη denotes experienced states, passions, or afflictions.

passages.text: For example, Adam, who came into being according to his likeness, is created blind, is handed down as possessing no knowledge of good or evil, is found to be a transgressor, is expelled from Paradise, and is punished with death. Likewise, the one who formed him, since he does not see from every direction, says at the destruction of Sodom, “Come, and after going down let us see whether they are carrying matters through in accordance with their outcry that is coming to me; but if not, so that I may know,” and thereby shows himself to be ignorant. As for his saying about Adam, “Let us cast him out, lest, after stretching out his hand, he touch the tree of life and eat, and he will live forever”—his saying “lest perhaps” indicates ignorance, while his further statement, “perhaps, after eating, he will live forever,” indicates envy as well. That it is written, “God considered that he had made the human being,” means that he both changes his mind and is ignorant. For “considered” is a reflection by which someone, through ignorance, wishes to determine precisely the outcome of what he intends, or the reflection of someone regretting something that did not turn out according to his intention. That it is written, “And the Lord smelled an odor of fragrance,” belongs to one who is needy, while taking pleasure in the fatty smoke of meats belongs to one who is not good. Testing—as it is written, “And the Lord tested Abraham”—belongs to one who is evil and ignorant of the outcome of the endurance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γνῶσιν ἀγαθοῦ ἢ κακοῦ οὐκ ἔχων παραδέδοται
lexical_decisions.chosen: is handed down as possessing no knowledge of good or evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect passive παραδέδοται can describe how Adam is transmitted or represented in the received account; “is delivered over” is possible but less coherent here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since he does not see from every direction
lexical_decisions.rationale: The literal spatial image of πανταχόθεν is retained rather than replaced outright with “is not omniscient.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: lest perhaps / perhaps
lexical_decisions.rationale: After a preventive command μήπως means “lest,” but Simon isolates it as an expression of uncertainty, effectively “perhaps”; the translation preserves both contextual forces.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he both changes his mind and is ignorant
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here μετανοεῖ is an accusation of divine reconsideration or regret, not moral-spiritual reorientation toward God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the fatty smoke of meats
lexical_decisions.rationale: κνίση is the steam, smoke, or savor produced by burning fat or flesh; “savory odor” would soften the polemical physical image.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the outcome of the endurance
lexical_decisions.rationale: τέλος can denote either the outcome or the limit of endurance; “outcome” best fits the claim that testing seeks information.

source_issues.issue: The grave accent on μὲ is an apparent accentuation irregularity in the printed reading. The intended pronoun “me” is nevertheless clear and the wording is translatable without restoring any missing content.

passages.text: Similarly, Simon appeared, by many things from the Scriptures, to demonstrate that God is subject to every passion. In response Peter said, “If an evil and utterly wicked person has no desire to expose himself concerning the things in which he sins, answer me.” Simon said, “He does not.” Peter said, “How, then, can God be evil and wicked, if the evil things publicly written against him were added by his own will?” Simon replied, “It is possible that, contrary to his intention, the exposure written against him came from another power.” Peter said, “First, then, let us investigate this. If he exposed himself by his own counsel, as you already agreed, he is not wicked. But if it was done by another power, the matter must be investigated—and with all our strength. It must be examined whether someone has subjected him, though he alone is good, to all these evil things.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: Similarly
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁμῶς can mean “likewise” or “in the same way,” linking this summary to Simon’s preceding examples.

lexical_decisions.chosen: has no desire to expose himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀγαπᾷ with the infinitive concerns willingness or desire, while ἐλέγχειν here means exposing or convicting one’s own wrongdoing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by his own will
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contextual contrast with παρὰ προαίρεσιν and ὑπὸ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ βουλῆς supports understanding λείμματι as an orthographic form related to λῆμα, “will” or “resolve.” Taken formally from λείμμα, it could instead suggest “deficiency” or “omission,” which fits the argument poorly.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the exposure written against him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔλεγχος can mean refutation, censure, or exposure; “exposure” maintains the connection with God’s alleged self-disclosure of blameworthy traits.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μή τις αὐτὸν μόνον ἀγαθὸν ὄντα ἐπὶ πᾶσιν τοῖς κακοῖς ὑπέβαλεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: whether someone has subjected him, though he alone is good, to all these evil things
lexical_decisions.rationale: μή introduces the matter to be examined, while ὑποβάλλειν ἐπί can mean subjecting someone to charges or adverse representations.

source_issues.issue: The printed form ordinarily points to λείμμα, “remainder, deficiency, or omission,” but the immediate contrasts with “contrary to his intention” and “by his own counsel” strongly suggest an orthographic form of λήματι from λῆμα, “will” or “resolve.” The contextual interpretation is defensible, but the unusual printed spelling is disclosed rather than silently normalized.
